While much of this commercial EV load already occurs during the day—when dynamic price signals may be less impactful—the exclusion of non-residential EV load leaves a gap in assessing the full price response potential of EVs. In future work, updates to the baseline model can streamline the ability to holistically model the charging demands of individually-owned LDEVs. Further, the dispatch model used for LDEVs here could be applied to fleet vehicles and medium-heavy duty electric vehicles with additional research and development. 4.5.4 Behavioral considerations A critical area for future work is better understanding the behavioral considerations that impact the adoption and the effectiveness of dynamic electricity pricing. This study focused on the technical potential and cost effectiveness of price response, assuming customers are already on dynamic tariffs, and therefore does not capture the myriad complexities involved. Tariff adoption, for example, is influenced not only by the promise of bill savings but also by factors such as the types of end uses a customer has, their income level, and how well they understand the benefits of dynamic pricing. Customers with higher energy consumption or specific appliances like electric vehicles or heat pumps may have more to gain, but customers with lower incomes may be less likely to adopt these tariffs if they are concerned about bill volatility. Future work should explore how these different variables influence tariff adoption rates. Technology adoption is another crucial factor. Many of the potential benefits of dynamic pricing depend on customers having the right enabling technologies, such as smart thermostats, battery storage systems, or smart appliances. However, adoption rates for these technologies are uneven and depend on a variety of factors, including upfront costs, perceived benefits, and ease of use. Customers may also face barriers such as a lack of awareness about available technologies, distrust of automated systems, or concerns about privacy and control. This uneven technology adoption will affect how much flexibility can be achieved through dynamic tariffs, as only customers with the right equipment can fully participate. The third major behavioral factor is usage—the extent to which customers are willing to enable the necessary features of their smart devices and adjust their settings to participate in demand response. Even when customers adopt enabling technologies, they may not use them to their full potential. For instance, they may override automated responses or fail to enable dynamic 65 pricing settings if doing so affects their comfort or convenience. Additionally, many customers may not regularly adjust their energy use patterns even when financial incentives are present. This highlights the need for more detailed exploration of how customer behavior impacts the actual performance of dynamic pricing programs. Given the complexity of human behavior, a significant amount of additional research is needed to refine models that estimate customer adoption and response under dynamic pricing schemes. Future work should include more detailed behavioral studies, pilot programs, and surveys to better understand the drivers and barriers to tariff and technology adoption, as well as customer engagement with dynamic pricing features.
